title: Iran proposes temporary Hormuz plan giving itself greater control over transit lines
description: DUBAI, July 28 (Reuters) - Iran has proposed to Oman a temporary arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under which one direction of traffic would pass through Iranian waters and part of the
fullText:
DUBAI, July 28 (Reuters) - Iran has proposed to Oman a temporary arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz ‌under which one direction of traffic would pass through Iranian ‌waters and part of the opposite route would also be in Iranian waters, ​Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state television on Tuesday.

Gharibabadi said Tehran rejected an Omani proposal for an equal division of transit routes between the two countries, saying such a plan did ‌not address Tehran's security ⁠concerns until long-term regional stability is achieved.

He said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed if Muscat ⁠rejected Iran's proposal, adding that Tehran had never recognised the southern route along Oman's coast.

Gharibabadi also said Tehran had made it clear ​to Muscat ​that it no longer recognised ​the Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS), ‌arguing that this pathway roughly in the middle of the waterway lies mostly within Omani waters and runs contrary to Iran's need to monitor transiting vessels after being attacked by the U.S. and Israel in late February.

The TSS, adopted by the International Maritime ‌Organization, is currently unusable due to ​the risk of mines and has ​been replaced with Iran's ​northern route and Oman's southern route.

"This is for ‌national security and not bullying because ​when the TSS ​was for 60 years in Omani waters, we didn't say anything," Gharibabadi said.

The Iranian diplomat also warned that Tehran ​would not allow ‌any third country, even if invited by Oman, to de-mine ​the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Court panel declines to block Trump's mail ballot order, but its status for midterms remains unclear
description: A federal appellate panel on Tuesday refused to block President Donald Trump's executive order seeking to restrict mail voting, a day after the administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in ...
fullText:
A federal appellate panel on Tuesday refused to block President Donald Trump's executive order seeking to restrict mail voting, a day after the administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on the proposal in a separate case.

The three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld a May ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Carl J. Nichols that said an injunction against the order was premature. Nichols ruled that the Democrats and voting rights groups who challenged the order couldn't seek the injunction until the Trump administration issued formal regulations governing it. The administration started releasing those directives days later.

The circuit court panel, with two judges appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama and one by Trump, found that was proper and there were no noted dissents. But the unsigned decision noted that if the administration truly tried to force such changes in the few months remaining before November's midterm election, it may well get halted by courts.

"The action the Order contemplates would involve the President, whom the Constitution vests with no express authority over the conduct of elections, undertaking a substantial and unfunded overhaul of election procedures — including the implementation of a nationwide reform to Postal Service mail-handling processes —on the threshold of the November election. Put differently, the Order 'may not prove feasible to implement in any manner whatsoever,'" said the ruling, quoting a prior legal opinion.

In a separate case filed by Democratic state officials, a federal judge in Massachusetts last month blocked the executive order from taking effect for this year's elections because it was already forcing states, which are granted the power under the U.S. Constitution to control their own elections, to revise their procedures on the fly. That ruling was upheld on Saturday by a Boston-based appeals court and then was appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday by the Trump administration.

The Postal Service did not immediately respond to questions about what action it's taking related to Trump's executive order. But the union representing postal workers, which opposes having its members implement the order, said Tuesday that its members are being directed to prepare an online portal through which voters will have to submit information to be eligible for mail ballots.

"The IT people in the background are moving forward with creating the portals to make sure that we can accomplish the task if given to us," American Postal Workers Union President Jonathan Smith said in a telephone interview.

Trump has repeatedly tried to unilaterally change voting procedures since he took office for the second time, only to be blocked by the courts. The push follows years of lies about vote fraud to try to explain away the president's loss to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020.

In his March executive order, Trump directed the federal government to create a list of eligible voters and the U.S. Postal Service to deliver ballots only to those on that list. Lawsuits noted that the Constitution grants states control of their elections, not the president, and that Congress can pass laws changing procedures for federal elections but has not done so.

Trump signed another executive order on elections last year, just months after taking office, that would impose a nationwide voter ID requirement and force anyone registering to vote to provide documents proving they are U.S. citizens. Trump also is pushing Congress to pass a sweeping voting bill that would impose the documentary proof of citizenship requirement, but it has stalled in the Senate as it faces opposition from Democrats and some lawmakers from his own party.

title: Family facing homelessness due to succession rule
description: A housing association says it cannot pass the tenancy from a deceased person to their relatives.
fullText:
A man says he and his family are facing homelessness after being asked to leave a housing association property following the death of his parents.

Mario and Leonio di Blasi moved into Mario's mother's home in the Wedmore Vale area of Bristol in 2022 to care for her after the sudden death of his father.

But weeks after his mother's death in March 2025, the couple were surprised to be told the tenancy could not be passed to them.

A spokesperson for Brighter Places said the family's case had "been considered carefully and reviewed by managers" but it had to "balance compassion with our legal and regulatory responsibilities to ensure homes are allocated fairly and in line with policy".

Mario, whose parents had lived at the property since 2005, told the BBC he had been signed off from his job at Bristol Waste with stress due to the uncertainty of their housing situation.

"It's just always going through your mind, there's never a break. It's every day, all you think about," he said.

Hospital emergency department closed after fire

Hopes new hourly train service could be expanded

Council house tenants face 'stealth rent hikes'

Leoni said the family had "no other choice" than to move into her disabled mother-in-law's home to care for her, and had asked about the terms of the tenancy in the event of her death.

According to Brighter Places' succession policy, there is no legal right for people living in the property to stay after the death of a tenant if the deceased was already a successor to the tenancy.

The housing association does have a discretionary succession process, which it said it follows on a case by case basis.

However, the di Blasi's said they had been told their needs did not meet the criteria.

Mario said: "It's just everything, [all the] memories... it's a home for us as well, it's a safe place really.

"Now we've made it our home, it's just getting taken off us. It's just not a nice feeling at all."

Leoni said the housing association told them to contact Bristol City Council after leaving their property.

"They're supposed to help the community no matter where you've come from, or who you are, or what your background is - you are supposed to help people with housing," she said.

"They haven't helped us, they've just told us to go."

The family of four have started a legal challenge against their eviction, with their next court date set for 18 August.

But they said it has been impossible for them to make plans for the future.

"Are we going to be here this Christmas or is this our last summer here? [It's] little things like, do I do the garden? because I might not be here," Leoni said.

Katrina Eastgate, from the renters union ACORN who have taken up the di Blasi's case, said the family had been through "such a hard time" and she was hoping for a "good outcome".

"We know [Brighter Places] have got to meet their obligations, we know that they've got their own rights and responsibilities and stuff like that," she said.

"All we're asking is for them to see the people who are looking at losing their home.

"A lot of people are dealing with this at a time where they're losing a loved one and it feels like there's a real lack of compassion in some of these processes and procedures that don't acknowledge that someone's just lost a parent, maybe two."

A spokesperson for Brighter Places said they had responded to correspondence from parties acting on behalf of the family, including their MP, a councillor and a third-party advocate, and had reviewed the case a number of times.

"Following these reviews, our decision has remained unchanged," they said, adding that it would not be appropriate to comment further due to the ongoing legal process.

title: EBay, former executives to pay $56 million to settle couple's harassment case
description: EBay and three former top executives have agreed to pay $55.7 million to resolve a lawsuit by a Massachusetts couple who fell victim to a bizarre stalking and
fullText:
July 28 (Reuters) - EBay and three former top executives have agreed to pay $55.7 million to resolve a lawsuit by a Massachusetts couple who fell victim to a bizarre stalking and harassment ‌campaign carried out by several of its employees in retaliation for their coverage of the e-commerce company in ‌a newsletter they publish.

How much did eBay pay to settle the lawsuit?

What was the eBay stalking campaign against Massachusetts couple?

Which executives were involved in the harassment scheme?

What criminal charges did eBay employees face?

David and Ina Steiner announced the settlement late on Monday, bringing an end to a case they filed in 2021 in ​Boston federal court after several former eBay employees were prosecuted for targeting them in a cyber-stalking campaign that involved sending the couple cockroaches, fly larvae and a bloody Halloween pig mask.

As part of the settlement, eBay agreed to pay $46.15 million to the couple; fund $6 million in charitable contributions to nonprofit organizations; and issue a "strongly-worded" statement about the conduct of three of its top ‌former executives.

"We believe this resolution sends a ⁠clear message that corporations and their executives cannot engage in this type of misconduct without facing significant consequences," Christopher Murphy, the Steiners' attorney, said in a statement.

EBay in a statement said ⁠that what happened to the Steiners was "wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened."

"We continue to extend our deepest apologies to the Steiners," the company said. "This agreement is consistent with our commitment to fairly compensate the Steiners and fulfills our efforts to make things ​right."

Seven former ​eBay workers pleaded guilty and received sentences of as high ​as 57 months in prison for participating in ‌the scheme, which also involved several of them traveling from California to Natick, Massachusetts, to surveil the Steiners and try to install a GPS tracking device on their car.

Prosecutors have said was aim was to silence them after senior executives deemed their newsletter, EcommerceBytes, critical of the company. The campaign began after then-CEO Devin Wenig in August 2019 texted Steve Wymer, then its chief communications officer, that it was time to "take her down," referring to Ina Steiner, according to prosecutors ‌and the Steiners.

EBay itself was criminally charged and agreed in 2024 ​to pay a $3 million fine.

Wenig, a former Thomson Reuters executive who stepped ​down as eBay's CEO in September 2019, was never ​charged. His lawyers did not respond to a request for comment but have argued he ‌had no knowledge or any involvement in the ​harassment campaign.

As part of the settlement, ​the Steiners' attorneys said Wenig will pay them $2 million and make a $1 million donation to a charity focused on protecting First Amendment rights in the name of Ina Steiner.

title: Talarico pulls ahead of Paxton by 5-points in new Texas Senate race poll
description: A new poll shows Democrat James Talarico leading Republican Ken Paxton by 5 points in the Texas Senate race. Here's a deeper look into what we know.
fullText:
A little over four months before Election Day, the Texas Senate race to replace U.S. Sen. John Cornyn remains contentious, as a new poll shows the Democratic candidate has opened a 5-point lead over the Republican candidate.

The Texas Public Opinion Research (TPOR) released a new poll on Tuesday, July 28, showing Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton trailing Democratic Texas state Rep. James Talarico.

The poll comes after two other polls in late June showed Paxton and Talarico tied within each poll's margin of error.

Here's a deeper look into the Texas Senate poll from TPOR.

The poll was conducted from July 15-17, polling 1,048 likely Texas voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. It was conducted by TPOR, which labels itself as a nonpartisan public opinion research group. Democratic strategist Luke Warford directs it.

The poll found that Talarico (45%) leads Paxton (40%) by 5 points in the U.S. Senate race — a 2-point increase from TPOR's post-runoff poll in May — with Talarico continuing to retain strong support from moderates and independents.

The poll also found that Talarico's performance is driven by voters saying Talarico better understands the economic challenges working Texans face than Paxton by 7 points, and that they trust Talarico to address affordability issues over Paxton by a 9-point margin.

However, the poll also found that 14% of Texas voters remain undecided, with 19% leaning toward Paxton, 10% toward Talarico, and 5% toward Libertarian Ted Brown.

Among Black and Latino voters, Talarico is strongly favored, leading Black voters by 63 points (71% to 8%) and Latino voters by 46 points (66% to 20%). Paxton, on the other hand, leads among white voters by 20 points (53% to 33%).

The poll was done days after The Texas Tribune and ProPublica published a joint investigation on July 7 alleging that Paxton had voted in six elections in the past two years using a former address. This led the Collin County Democratic Party to file a complaint on July 14 with the state's chief elections officer to determine whether Paxton had violated the state's election laws.

Paxton's campaign told USA TODAY on July 17 that it disputes the allegations made in the investigation and that Paxton is a "lawful, registered Texas voter in full compliance with the law."

Before this poll, two polls in June showed the race was deadlocked.

A New York Times/Siena poll, published on June 30, shows Paxton tied at 47% with Talarico.

The poll comes after a June 23 poll from the University of Texas and the Texas Politics Project that showed Paxton at 43% and Talarico at 42%, a 1-point gap within the survey's margin of error.

Mateo Rosiles is the Texas Connect reporter for USA TODAY and its regional papers in Texas. Got a news tip for him? Email him at mrosiles@usatodayco.com.

description: , Nayera Abdallah and Elwely Elwelly WASHINGTON/DUBAI, July 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the United States was having "good talks" with Iran and there was a
fullText:
WASHINGTON/DUBAI, July 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the United States was having "good talks" with Iran and there was a chance of a deal over their conflict, but he warned that U.S. strikes would resume if the negotiations failed to deliver.

Despite Trump's optimism, Tehran appeared to quickly test the pause ‌in the U.S. military campaign, with Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq reporting drone attacks on Monday.

Washington abruptly suspended a two-week campaign of air strikes on Iran on Saturday in Trump's latest ‌strategic U-turn in the five-month-old conflict.

"We're having good talks," he said. "I think there's a good chance that something could happen, and if it does, good, if it doesn't, we go back to doing what we were doing two days ago."

At a campaign rally in ​Michigan later on Monday, Trump said of Iran: "You can't bribe them. You've got to beat them, and we'll beat the hell out of them. But we'll see how it turns out. Right now, there are very friendly negotiations going on."

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday that messages were still being passed between the sides through mediators and Iran had not forsaken diplomacy, but reports that it requested negotiations were "fabricated."

"This is not in our DNA," he said.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Sunday that Iran would halt its own attacks as long as Trump's self-imposed ceasefire continued.

Iran's central military command later on Monday accused the U.S. of threatening vessels and ‌oil tankers in its territorial waters and of "attempting to implement an illegal maritime ⁠blockade", which it said "constitutes an escalation of the conflict in the region."

Saudi Arabia said it shot down drones aimed at petroleum targets, including in Riyadh. It said they had been launched from Iraq by Iran-backed armed groups, and it reserved the right to respond.

Separately, Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said they had targeted the East-West ⁠Pipeline carrying oil to Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea port of Yanbu in retaliation for Saudi drone incursions.

Tehran also said it remained in control of the contested Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for global energy supplies, which Trump has demanded vessels be able to pass through freely.

Public disapproval of the war has been weighing on Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections in which they have to defend slim congressional majorities.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll ​conducted ​over the weekend showed Trump's approval rating ticking higher to 37%, up three points from last month when it tied ​the lowest of his presidency.

However, just one in three Americans support the Iran war, ‌the lowest Reuters/Ipsos reading since the conflict's early days, with most saying Trump has failed to explain his goals.

The end of the U.S. campaign after 13 successive nights of intensifying bombing and Trump's remarks on talks sent oil prices tumbling. U.S. crude CLc1 fell 8.21% to $81.98 a barrel, and Brent LCOc1 fell to $87.77 per barrel, down 9.31% on the day.

Trump's decision to suspend U.S. attacks reflected advice from his military that the bombing had reached the limits of what it could achieve, according to a U.S. official and several U.S. media reports.

The U.S. official told Reuters military commanders had advised the president they were running out of targets and that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had expressed concern over the depletion of air munitions.

Trump dismissed suggestions that the U.S. faced munitions shortages, saying the military was rapidly rebuilding ‌inventories depleted by shipments to Ukraine. He said he would like more of "the more sophisticated stuff."

IRAN MEDIA SAY SIX SHIPS ​TURNED BACK

Iranian state media outlets cited an "informed source" as saying that Iran had turned around six "offending ships" on Monday that had ​attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without permission.

Trump launched his renewed bombing campaign to punish ​Iran after Tehran fired on ships using a route promoted by the United States, which told vessels to sail close to the coast of Oman.

Iran says ships may ‌pass only through a Hormuz channel that runs closer to its own coast, which ​it controls and where it intends to impose transit ​fees.

The two weeks of renewed U.S. bombing killed scores in Iran and destroyed bridges and tunnels across the south as well as military targets.

Four U.S. service members were killed in return fire against U.S. bases in neighbouring states. Iran also struck civilian infrastructure in Gulf countries, calling it retaliation for U.S. strikes.

It remains unclear what leverage Washington can exert to break Iran's grip on the ​strait.

Washington and Tehran reached an agreement in June on a framework for ‌talks meant to take place by the end of August to resolve major issues such as Iran's nuclear programme.

But they have disputed the meaning of the memorandum's language about the ​strait, with Washington insisting it requires Tehran to allow free travel, while Iran says it grants it the authority to supervise transit.

(Additional reporting by Muayad Hameed in Iraq. Writing by ​Peter Graff, Toby Chopra and David Brunnstrom; Editing by Sharon Singleton, Toby Chopra, Mark Potter and Cynthia Osterman)

title: Florida puts ex-police officer to death for girl's murder, first of 2 executions set for single day
description: A former police officer convicted of the on-duty rape and murder of a young girl was put to death Tuesday, the first of two lethal injections planned for a single day in Florida, hours before an 80-ye...
fullText:
STARKE, Fla. (AP) — A former police officer convicted of the on-duty rape and murder of a young girl was put to death Tuesday, the first of two lethal injections planned for a single day in Florida, hours before an 80-year-old man was to become the second-oldest inmate executed in modern U.S. history.

Tuesday marked the first time since two convicted murderers were executed on a single day — in Arkansas in 2017 — that a state has planned virtually back-to-back executions. It also comes 18 months after Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis began stepping up executions at a pace unseen in Florida since the U.S. death penalty was reinstated in 1976, making his the busiest death chamber in the nation.

Since the beginning of 2025, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions in the U.S.

James Aren Duckett, 68, was pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. The 11th inmate executed by the state this year, Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning an 11-year-old girl while working as a police officer in a small central Florida city in 1987.

Duckett declined to make a final statement, responding "no sir" when asked. About 4 minutes after the execution began, the prison's warden shook Duckett and shouted his name, but there was no response.

Later Tuesday, barring any last-minute development, 80-year-old Dominick Anthony Occhicone was scheduled to become the oldest prisoner executed in Florida's modern history starting at 6 p.m. Occhicone was convicted of killing his ex-girlfriend's parents in 1986.

Until Tuesday, a total of 17 executions had been carried out in the U.S. so far this year, with Florida leading the way with more executions than all other states combined.

Both men had made last-ditch appeals to the U.S. Supreme Court, and last week, the Florida Supreme Court denied appeals by both men to intervene.

Duckett's attorneys had unsuccessfully claimed Duckett's innocence and argued the state's handling of the DNA evidence is the reason for the inconclusive results.

Occhicone's attorneys had argued that several age-related ailments, including kidney and prostate problems, could make his execution especially painful, constituting cruel and unusual punishment.

DeSantis hasn't said why he scheduled two executions six hours apart. A Florida prison official said Tuesday morning that the department was confident in its readiness to carry out both executions. All Florida executions are by injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw a record 19 executions in 2025, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the reinstatement of the death penalty in the U.S. in 1976. The previous high was eight executions set in 2014.

Florida has executed 29 people since the beginning of 2025 while the rest of the U.S. states combined have carried out 35 executions over the same time frame.

If the day's final execution is carried out Tuesday evening, that would bring total executions for DeSantis' final two years in office to 31 overall, compared to just nine executions during his first six years in office. With another execution set for August, 2026 could also be a record-breaking year.

Nationwide, it's not uncommon for two different states to hold executions on the same date, but it's less common for a single state to perform two in a day. Before Florida, Arkansas last executed two inmates on the same day by lethal injection three hours apart in April 2017. And Texas executed two convicted killers on the same day in 2000, the year the state executed 40 prisoners.

Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty urged DeSantis ahead of Tuesday to halt both executions.

"July 28 represents an unprecedented escalation of Florida's use of the death penalty," the group's executive director, Grace Hanna, said in a statement. "These are two profoundly different cases, but they point to the same troubling reality: Florida continues to expand the use of capital punishment, despite mounting evidence that it is not what Floridians want."

DeSantis has rarely commented on the pace of executions, but previously said that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.

"Some of these crimes were committed in the '80s," the governor said last year. "Justice delayed is justice denied. I felt I owed it to them to make sure this ran very smoothly. If I honestly thought someone was innocent, I would not pull the trigger."

If his execution proceeds as planned, Occhicone would become the state's oldest inmate to be executed just weeks after two 74-year-old men briefly held that spot, the second man just a week older than the first at his time of death.

Occhicone also would become the second-oldest prisoner known to be put to death in modern U.S. history after 83-year-old Walter Moody Jr. was executed in Alabama in 2018 for a wave of southern mail bombs in 1989 that killed a federal judge and wounded a Black civil rights attorney.

DeSantis initially signed a death warrant for Duckett in February, scheduling his execution for March 31. But the Florida Supreme Court issued a stay just days before the planned execution to allow for DNA testing of old evidence that couldn't be performed at the time of the original trial because of technological limitations. The results came back inconclusive, meaning that they did not exonerate Duckett or definitively connect him to the crime. Judges have allowed the jury verdict to stand.

When Occhicone's death warrant was signed late last month, his was the only execution scheduled for Tuesday. But after the Florida Supreme Court removed Duckett's stay on July 8, DeSantis signed a new death warrant on July 14 and added Duckett to Occhicone's execution date, which hadn't been done in Florida in more than 60 years. Florida Department of Corrections records show multiple executions on a single day were more common in the past, with the last being on May 12, 1964.

title: DSA co-chair mocked for proudly confirming socialists want to abolish the Senate, national borders, prisons
description: DSA co-chair confirmed abolishing the Senate, prisons, borders, and ICE on live TV, sparking fierce backlash from Mike Johnson, Ted Cruz and more.
fullText:
The national co-chair for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) was mocked by conservatives on Sunday after she proudly confirmed many of the DSA's policy ideas, including abolishing the Senate, eliminating prisons and getting rid of national borders, among others.

Speaking to Fox News' Shannon Bream, Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) national co-chair Megan Romer fired off a series of "yes" and "true" responses when asked whether the organization's platform calls for dismantling major American institutions.

"[You're advocating for] abolish[ing] the Senate?" Bream asked.

Romer also affirmed the organization's support for replacing the presidency and Supreme Court, abolishing ICE, eventually eliminating national borders while granting amnesty to people living in the country illegally, defunding the Pentagon, phasing out prisons and shifting most large corporations to public ownership.

She said some proposals, including abolishing borders and prisons, are part of the organization's long-term vision.

Watch: House Dems Dodge Questions On Socialist Agenda That Threatens To Abolish Key Institutions

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, wrote, "These people are insane."

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson said in a post of the exchange on Fox News, "Read their platform: Abolish the Senate, the Presidency, the Supreme Court and immigration enforcement. Open the border wide. Grant mass amnesty. Defund the Pentagon. The barbarians are inside the gate—and Democrats are WELCOMING them in! Communism is no longer a far-fetched threat. It is here on our SHORES! This isn't just Common Sense vs. Crazy anymore. It's Common Sense vs. COMMUNISM."

Actress Patricia Heaton wrote, "Yikes."

Dsa Member Leads Dem Primary In Midwest Battleground But Trails Likely Gop Nominee: Poll

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., wrote, "The DSA isn't just gaining influence in New York or California. Bernie Sanders- and Mamdani-backed candidates are winning races across the country. Watch this clip closely. These ideas could be coming to your community sooner than you think."

Rep. Burgess Owens, R-Utah, said in response, "Love that today's Marxist[s] are so 'in your face' honest. This proves the ole saying… ignorance is Bliss."

Tom Tiffany, a Republican running for governor in Wisconsin, said the remarks from Romer sounded like democratic socialist Francesca Hong, who is running in the state's Democratic gubernatorial primary.

"This sounds a lot like DSA-backed @FrancescaHongWI. Does she want to abolish the police? Yep. Does she want to abolish prisons? Absolutely. Did she call for abolishing the U.S. Senate? Yes. Socialism is knocking on Wisconsin's door. This November, we slam it shut," Tiffany wrote.

When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Hong rejected Tiffany's accusations.

"Tom Tiffany is once again telling lies and inventing quotes, because he can't run on his record. Rep. Hong has never called for abolishing the U.S. Senate. Tiffany cannot produce a single statement where she did, because it doesn't exist. She has spoken about police and prison abolition in the past as an aspirational goal, but it is not her current position, and it's not something she will pursue as governor. She does not support replacing the presidency with the Supreme Court. Eliminating national borders isn't her position either, and it's not even part of the official DSA platform. DSA is a membership organization, not a political party. Rep. Hong is not endorsed by DSA national, and doesn't agree with everything in its national program," Hong communications director Allison Geyer told Fox News Digital.

Hong's campaign website lists the Milwaukee, Northeast Wisconsin and Madison DSA chapters on her endorsement page.

Hong posted "Abolish the Senate" to X in February 2021.

"Democrat Socialist Francesca Hong can try to rewrite her record, but she can't rewrite her own words calling to abolish the police, ICE, and even the U.S. Senate. Her ideas are so radical that her own campaign has to lie and pretend she never said them," a Tiffany campaign spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Hong previously appeared on far-left streamer Hasan Piker's show and distanced herself from the streamer during an MS NOW interview in early July.

"I condemn hatred, discrimination, antisemitism and Islamophobia, any sort of dehumanizing of communities," Hong said during the interview. "Being on these streams, it's important that we get our message out in places where, you know, campaigns struggle to reach voters. Just because I am on a platform certainly does not mean that I endorse everything that has been said by either the hosts or other people who have gone on."

Joe Mitchell, a Republican running for Congress in Iowa, accused Lindsay James, a Democrat running for the same seat, of standing for the same policy positions.

".@Lindsay4Iowa stands for all of this," he wrote.

"No, Lindsay does not support any of these out of touch, ridiculous, policies. Lobbyist Joe Mitchell is lying about Lindsay again because Joe knows his record of enriching himself at Iowans' expense is disqualifying," Jackson Smith, a spokesperson for James' campaign, told Fox News Digital when reached for comment.

The Virginia GOP also demanded all Democrats be asked if they support the policies put forth by the DSA.

"This is what Virginia Democrats think belongs under their 'big tent.' Every Democrat should be asked to explicitly denounce these insane anti-American positions & the DSA. If they refuse to do so, we know where they stand," they wrote on X.

GOP Tennessee Rep. Chuck Fleischmann wrote in response to Romer's statements, "The DSA is a complete inversion of what America stands for; you can watch it for yourself. Their movement is a coordinated effort to undermine our nation's values and dismantle the freedoms we hold dear. If we don't stand up, speak out, and defend our country's core values, we could soon find ourselves watching the America we love slip away."

Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman also called out Romer's comments on X.

He wrote, "This isn't a big tent—it's anarchy. Why can't Dems call out the DSA?"

"This is insane. How can anyone vote for a @DemSocialists member unless you are an anarchist?" Bill Ackman asked on X.

Ackman has been outspoken about New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's democratic socialist vision for the Big Apple.

He called his policies a "disaster" for the city, and said he wasn't a fan of the mayor.

The DSA did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

Socialist platforms and campaigns are on the rise across the country, including in New York, where two House candidates backed by Mamdani defeated incumbent progressive lawmakers and will likely sail to victory in the November general election.

A third open House race saw a Mamdani-backed candidate defeat an establishment-backed Democrat.

Fox News' Taylor Penley contributed to this report.

description: Holocaust Museum Chairman Jeff Miller invited Zohran Mamdani to visit and learn what genocide actually means after the NYC mayor's repeated use of the term.
fullText:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is yet to publicly respond to an invitation from a prominent Holocaust museum to visit in order to "truly understand" what "genocide looks like" as he faces criticism from the Jewish community for repeatedly using that label to describe the situation in Gaza.

"You keep using the word 'genocide' when talking about Israel," Jeff Miller, chair of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, posted on X on Friday, inviting Mamdani to visit the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C.

"If you truly want to understand what genocide looks like, as Chairman of the United States Holocaust Memorial Council, I would be happy to personally arrange a tour of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum for you."

Miller was responding to a post from the UJA-Federation of New York expressing grief over a pair of recent stabbings in New York City carried out by an attacker who allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" during the attacks. Authorities say one of the victims is Jewish, and the attack is being investigated as a hate crime.

Jewish Leaders Fault Mamdani Rhetoric As Upper West Side Stabbing, Hate Crime Probe Continues

Miller's post went on to say that "words matter especially from elected leaders" and that "rhetoric that demonizes Israel and the Jewish state has consequences."

"I hope you are simply ignoring the impact of your words and not purposely trying to normalize antisemitism," Miller wrote. "My invitation is sincere. Come to the Museum. Learn what genocide actually means."

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office multiple times inquiring whether the mayor intends to take Miller up on his offer but did not receive a response.

Suspect Arrested After Allegedly Yelling 'Allahu Akbar,' Stabbing 2 Men In Nyc Attack

Miller told Fox News Digital that he felt an "obligation" to speak up and that he would be "happy" to personally walk Mamdani through the museum.

"If the mayor wants to repeatedly invoke that word, I invite him to come with me to the Holocaust Museum and confront what genocide actually looked like: the systematic attempt to annihilate an entire people," Miller said. "If he does not want to come to our museum, he should visit Rwanda or another place whose people have endured genocide and listen to survivors."

Miller added that Mamdani is free to "criticize the Israeli government" and disagree with policies, "but there is a profound difference between legitimate criticism of a government and rhetoric that demonizes the world's only Jewish state and helps normalize hostility toward Jews."

Miller's invitation was celebrated by many on social media, including Republican Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who posted on X that he hopes Mamdani takes the offer.

Mamdani's Latest Netanyahu Remarks Deepen Concerns Among Jewish Leaders

"The US Holocaust Memorial Museum — where I proudly serve on the Council — is an important institution that shows the truth about what happened," Scott wrote. "I urge anyone visiting Washington, DC to stop by. "

"The @NYCMayor Mamdani should take up the Chairman's offer for a tour of the Holocaust Museum so he understands what is genocide," billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman posted on X.

Mamdani has faced intense criticism for his position on Israel since jumping into the mayoral race last year and since taking office, he has often angered the Jewish community with comments calling for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and repeatedly accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza after the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack.

"Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people," Mamdani said last week in a video announcement that he did not have the authority to arrest Netanyahu in accordance with an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant, a warrant the United States does not recognize.

"He is responsible for the killing of more than 73,000 people, for the maiming of tens of thousands of children as those who survive undergo amputation without anesthesia. For the targeting of neonatal hospitals and maternity care centers, denying newborns even the chance to live. For the countless people he starved as he blocked food and humanitarian aid from reaching them. For the gunning down of hundreds of aid workers and journalists."

title: Mamdani sparks fears of violence after doxing wealthy NYC property owners: 'Outright dangerous'
description: The searchable database names affluent property owners who could face the proposed pied-à-terre tax, raising new privacy and security concerns.
fullText:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani opened a new front in his ongoing battle with New York City's wealthy after his administration published a searchable database identifying affluent property owners who could be subject to the city's proposed pied-à-terre tax, a move critics say could expose them to harassment and public safety risks.

The database, released by the city's Department of Finance, allows users to search properties and view the names and addresses of owners whose non-primary residences could be subject to the proposed tax. A spokesperson for the department said the publication of the property roll was required by state law.

"As per State law, a property roll was released for public inspection. From this list, DOF will identify properties that may be subject to the new non-primary residence property surcharge," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

A person familiar with the process, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the city has publicly released similar property tax rolls every year for many years in accordance with New York state law. The person said new taxes and surcharges follow the same process: The state passes legislation, a public property roll is published, and the Department of Finance identifies the properties subject to the levy using criteria established by the state.

Mamdani's Rent Freeze, Tax Hikes A 'One-two Wealth Destruction Punch,' Economists Warn

However, critics argue the database goes well beyond traditional public records by compiling the names and addresses of affluent property owners into a single, easily searchable location, potentially creating new privacy and security risks. The debate carries added weight in America's largest city, where public safety remains a persistent political issue and affluent residents have long cited crime as a top concern.

While property ownership records have long been public, opponents say the city's decision to aggregate them into a dedicated database could make wealthy homeowners more vulnerable to harassment and potential violence. City Hall has defended the database as a transparency tool designed to help property owners determine whether they could be affected by the proposed tax and understand how to seek an exemption.

"Nobody wants this database more than Mamdani's band of communist social media agitators salivating to harass Americans at every turn," "Ruthless" podcast co-host John Ashbrook warned, pointing out the database could easily become a tool for Mamdani's online supporters to target landlords and other property owners.

"They attack anybody who questions his decisions, and there's no question they'll harass every New Yorker who provides housing for a living," he continued.

Meanwhile, the Real Estate Board of New York President James Whelan argued that the database also illustrates how broadly the proposed tax could reach beyond the ultra-wealthy residents its supporters have emphasized. Although Mamdani initially promoted the proposal as a tax on secondary homes worth more than $5 million and owned by the "ultra-wealthy and global elites," the final rules use different Department of Finance valuation thresholds depending on the type of property. According to the New York Post, over 960,000 residences could be listed in the database, which makes it possible to search and download property owners' information, including their names and addresses.

"By publishing a database of properties that might be subject to this tax before the tax has even been enacted, City Hall has only added to the confusion surrounding this proposal," Whelan told Fox News Digital.

"What this database really demonstrates is that the second-home tax is far broader and more complicated than its supporters have suggested," he continued. "Policymakers should take a hard look at the many homeowners who could be swept in despite not fitting the profile of the ultra-wealthy residents this tax was supposedly designed to target."

Mamdani Thanks Same Billionaire He Targeted In Tax Video For Nypd Money

The database marks the latest flashpoint in Mamdani's increasingly contentious relationship with the city's wealthiest residents.

Earlier this year, the mayor stood outside Citadel founder Ken Griffin's 24,000-square-foot Central Park South penthouse, purchased for a record $238 million, to promote his proposal to raise taxes on second homes worth more than $5 million after previously criticizing the billionaire hedge fund manager over his personal wealth. The video singled out Griffin by name.

Griffin later called the video "creepy and weird," arguing it put him in harm's way because it highlighted his residence while promoting higher taxes on the wealthy.

Longtime Republican strategist Colin Reed argued that the database and Mamdani's broader rhetoric against wealthy New Yorkers could carry dangerous consequences amid heightened concerns about political violence.

"In this era of heightened political violence, this type of inflammatory and divisive rhetoric is not only reckless, but outright dangerous, especially from a public official who not that long ago pledged to be a mayor for all New Yorkers," Reed told Fox News Digital.

"It's bad enough that the mayor is demonizing success and upward mobility that has so long defined the American dream, and doing so within the city that has defined American capitalism," Reed continued. "But to do so by pitting various classes against one another is beneath the office he holds."

Chicago Knows What Happens When Ken Griffin Turns On A City, Now Mamdani May Find Out

The clash has also revived a broader debate over whether New York risks driving away the wealthy residents and businesses that have long underpinned its economy. Griffin, whose fortune Forbes estimates at roughly $50 billion, moved Citadel's global headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022 after years of criticizing the Windy City's tax policies, crime and business climate.

The departure marked Griffin's break from Chicago, where he built one of the world's largest hedge funds and helped cement the city as a global financial hub. He has since warned that New York could face similar consequences if policymakers pursue an agenda he believes is hostile to high-income residents and businesses.

The latest controversy comes as business leaders closely watch whether New York's political climate is becoming less welcoming to the financial industry and wealthy taxpayers that have long anchored the city's economy.

At the center of the debate is whether the city can ask more of its wealthiest residents without weakening the tax base that helps fund municipal government.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office asking why the administration chose to publish the searchable database rather than notify affected property owners privately and whether it conducted a legal or privacy review before making the information available online. The office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: NY Times reporter admits Trump's 'delusional' foes have wrongly written his political obituary many times

fullText:
New York Times reporter Jonathan Swan suggested during a "60 Minutes Australia" interview released last week that President Donald Trump has "Napoleonic" ambition and a political survivability that should humble journalists.

Swan and fellow Times reporter Maggie Haberman discussed their new book, "Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump," and Swan offered speculation on the rest of the president's term and cautioned other journalists to have some humility.

"So there's still a sense that, even if Democrats take the House from Trump, they really can't touch him," Swan said in the interview. "And, like you said, his family's made a lot of money. He's wealthier than he's ever been. He has immunity conferred by the Supreme Court. And there's no prospect, even if he does get impeached, there's no prospect of a conviction."

"I think Donald Trump's obituary has been written so many times — his political obituary — by so many people," Swan continued. "And by this point, if you don't have some humility around that, I think, you know, you're operating in a fairly delusional way. This is someone who has incredible survival capacities, who's able to regenerate himself, and he's still got two and a half years left as the most powerful man on the planet, with no intention of receding at all."

How Trump Survives: Battling The Media, Former Allies And Assassination Attempts

As he spoke about the future of Trump's term, he noted that the president's next step may be taking on the Cuban regime.

"So there are many things he could do," he said. "The most obvious in foreign policy is Cuba. They've been looking at potential regime change in Cuba, but who knows? It's a big world out there, and we don't want to start being pundits and prognosticating."

Swan also described a past encounter at the White House that he suggested speaks volumes about Trump's personal mindset and policies. As Trump met with Swan and Haberman, he had purportedly shown them a document he claimed was written by a historian.

"So it opens by saying Donald Trump is the most powerful man who's ever existed, ever lived on the planet, by far," Swan said. "And then it goes on to compare him to what Donald Trump said was, to us, the top ten. And it was Stalin, Mao, Hitler, Napoleon, Attila the Hun, Genghis Khan, the Caesars, Alexander the Great, Tamerlane ... there's probably one I'm missing."

Trump Aims To Reset War Powers Clock With Controversial Bid To Bypass Congress

"And it had nothing to do with morality," Swan continued. "The document didn't mention morality. It was about power and raw power."

The premise of the document, Swan said, was that Trump is the most powerful leader in history and is willing to use power in a way no previous president has done within their lifetime, which he noted was remarkably similar to the book he wrote about the administration.

Swan added further, "I think it's also that he wants to be a sort of Napoleonic ... you know, the person who only needs to be known by one name, who is the defining figure of our age. And so, when Trump thinks about himself in history, I don't think he's comparing himself to Bill Clinton or, you know, name your U.S. president — Eisenhower. I think it is to figures like Napoleon and that he wants to be the defining global figure of our age."

title: Fact check: Trump is approaching 10 years of telling his Michigan ‘Man of the Year’ lie
description: For three consecutive presidential campaigns, President Donald Trump regularly told the same lie when he spoke in the swing state of Michigan. Before he even entered politics, he claimed, he was named...
fullText:
For three consecutive presidential campaigns, President Donald Trump regularly told the same lie when he spoke in the swing state of Michigan. Before he even entered politics, he claimed, he was named "Man of the Year" in the state.

The problem: CNN and other media outlets repeatedly noted that this award did not exist. But Trump revived the tale once more near the end of a falsehood-filled economic speech in Michigan on Monday — and added an additional lie claiming that an initially skeptical media had eventually discovered the award story was correct.

"I was here 25 years ago, I got Man of the Year. They — oh, by the way, the press questioned that, and then they found out it was true, actually," Trump said with a chuckle. "And I made a speech, and all I talked about was why are you letting them steal your auto industry?"

Nope. This is yet another example of the fake history that has littered various Trump addresses this month.

Approaching 10 full years after Trump debuted the "Man of the Year" lie, nobody has ever been able to find any evidence for it. The state of Michigan does not give out a "Man of the Year" award, Trump has never lived in the state, and he and his team have never specified who or what entity supposedly gave him this award and when.

In 2023, after nearly seven years of debunkings of Trump's "Man of the Year" tales, a Republican group in Michigan created a "Man of the Decade" award and gave it to him.

But Trump made clear Monday that this is not what he was referring to, since he said he was talking about a "Man of the Year" honor he received decades ago. (Side note: in many previous tellings of the "Man of the Year" story, like one during his 2024 campaign, he has placed the supposed honor in the 2010s rather than the 2000s as he suggested Monday.)

Dave Trott, a former Republican congressman in Michigan who became a sharp critic of Trump, has offered the most plausible theory about the possible basis for Trump's made-up story. In 2019, Trott contacted CNN to note that Trump had suggested at an event two years prior that he had received the "Man of the Year" award at a 2013 Republican dinner in Michigan to which Trott had invited Trump to make a speech.

At that 2013 dinner, Trott gave Trump gifts that included a framed copy of the Gettysburg Address. But Trott emphatically noted that nobody gave Trump any "Man of the Year" award.

At least once, Trump has acknowledged that the idea of him receiving such an honor in Michigan before his time as a politician was bewildering.

"In fact, five or six years before I even thought about running, for whatever reason they named me Man of the Year in Michigan. I said, 'How come?' I didn't even understand it myself," he said at a 2019 rally in New Hampshire — then repeated, "But I was named Man of the Year."

title: Virginia university didn't know of student's conviction before campus shooting, report says
description: A Virginia university missed opportunities to learn of a student's terrorism-related conviction before the man opened fire in an ROTC class in March, injuring two students and killing an Army veteran ...
fullText:
RICHMOND, Va. (AP) — A Virginia university missed opportunities to learn of a student's terrorism-related conviction before the man opened fire in an ROTC class in March, injuring two students and killing an Army veteran who fought back with "extraordinary heroism," an investigative report released Tuesday found.

The federal probation officer working with Mohamed Bailor Jalloh, who spent eight years in prison for attempting to aid the Islamic State, did not share Jalloh's criminal background with Old Dominion University, despite the serious nature of the offense, according to the report, which was produced by the law firm Cooley on behalf of the university.

Jalloh, who also died in the March attack, had attended the public university in Norfolk beginning in 2007, was suspended in 2010 and reenrolled after his early release from prison in December 2024. He was readmitted to the school in May last year.

No federal or state law enforcement agency reported his prior conviction either, the report said.

State law prohibits the university from inquiring about student criminal history before admission or readmission, according to the report. The university could have asked readmitted students to voluntarily disclose their criminal history but did not at the time, the report said.

The university "had no knowledge of the risk Jalloh posed or his federal terrorism conviction," the report said. Had officials known, it's likely they would have sought his removal from campus, it said.

"Given that Virginia law requires universities to rely on student self-disclosure, it is even more important that other law enforcement agencies ensure that information that universities need to know to safeguard their students is shared with universities. This critical failure led to tragic consequences here," the report said.

Officials with the FBI, which the report said investigated Jalloh's original offense, didn't immediately respond to emailed requests for comment about the report's findings.

Paul Arnett, the chief U.S. probation officer for Virginia's eastern district federal court, reached briefly by phone, requested questions about the report's findings in writing, which the AP provided.

Jalloh, a former member of the Virginia National Guard, was sentenced to 11 years in prison after pleading guilty in 2017 to providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization, the Islamic State group, according to prison records. He completed a drug treatment program that allowed him early release from federal prison.

In March this year, Jalloh entered a classroom and asked whether it was an ROTC class. After students answered affirmatively, he opened fire, according to authorities and the report.

The university's president said the report also shed new light on the "extraordinary heroism and bravery" shown by the cadets and Lt. Col. Brandon Shah, the instructor who was killed.

Authorities and cadets who were in the room said they stabbed and disarmed Jalloh, the report said.

Shah "immediately grappled with the attacker, which allowed other brave students to come to his aid and many other students to escape unharmed," the report said.

Cadets tried to save Shah's life but he died at a hospital, the report said.

Family members of Shah could not immediately be reached for comment. An Old Dominion graduate and former Army pilot, he flew hundreds of hours on combat missions before returning to the university to lead the Army ROTC battalion, according to a biography published by the university.

While the report noted that the university's police department responded "almost immediately and effectively," it also recommended improvements to the university's safety and emergency response protocols.

"The campus community has my complete assurance that we will act quickly to fully implement Cooley's recommendations as we actively work to make our campus as safe and secure as possible," university President Brian O. Hemphill said in a statement.

title: Trump can’t stop shooting himself in the foot, as the stage looks set once again for Warsh to hold—if not hike—interest rates
description: “After months of upside inflation surprises, patience is wearing thin,” writes EY-Parthenon’s Gregory Daco.
fullText:
President Trump's campaign for lower interest rates in the U.S. faces another setback this week at the meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Wall Street analysts have generally come to the conclusion that the FOMC will hold rates steady, if not hike them—and Trump's own foreign policy is an underlying factor. 

The FOMC, led by central bank chairman Kevin Warsh, will meet Tuesday and Wednesday of this week to discuss progress toward its targets of maximum employment and inflation at 2%.

It is the latter task that has caused the Fed some difficulty over the past few years. At the time of writing, inflation stands at 3.5%—a drop from May to June, but still elevated compared with the start of the year and the Fed's target.

How is Trump's foreign policy affecting interest rates?

Why might the Fed hold or hike rates?

What credibility challenges does Fed Chair Warsh face?

How are Middle East conflicts impacting Fed decisions?

Part of that reading has come from higher fuel prices, up 15.7% from a year ago. While pressure in this category is beginning to fade (down 4.9% May to June), prices remain elevated as a result of conflict in the Middle East, choking global oil supply as a result.

There is little sign of a resolution between Washington and Tehran in sight. While the two sides are not currently engaged in active military conflict, as they have been over the past fortnight, no official ceasefire has been announced. While the fragile pause of fire allows space for diplomacy to proceed, neither side has indicated they will capitulate over control of the Strait of Hormuz—the key shipping lane in the movement of oil around the planet.

Trump's foreign policy is therefore standing in the way of Warsh's path to a cut—Wall Street analysts highlighted at the start of the week.

Bank of America's base case is for a hold this month, wrote chief U.S. economist Aditya Bhave and his team: "With markets now pricing nearly 10 [basis points] of hikes in July, Chair Warsh faces a difficult choice. Not hiking could challenge the Fed's credibility on inflation. But raising rates would go against his framework of looking through supply shocks.

"We think July is Warsh's call, as he has enough votes either way. He has strategic incentives to hike soon. We still expect three 25 bp hikes, in September, October, and December."

Warsh's—and by proxy, the Fed's—credibility is at the heart of the scrutiny the central bank is currently under. Following President Trump's unprecedented onslaught against Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell, politicians and analysts alike wondered what the Oval Office's nominee for chairman would do once he was installed in D.C.

The key question was whether Warsh would advocate for the lower rate the president is angling for, even if the data suggests otherwise. So far, this hasn't come to pass. But an aversion to hiking the base rate if appropriate to do so could similarly raise alarm.

The workload has increased so much she's currently looking to hire her first employee while she balances a full-time role with fulfilling about 25 to 30 orders a week.

To make her listings shine, Friday says she regularly lugs a portable power station to the storage unit to power steamers and irons after work, and is considering renting a studio apartment with other sellers to run their stores.

"There's always things to be cleaned," Friday says. "There's always orders to be packed. There's always orders to be accepted."

Pickle, a peer-to-peer luxury clothing rental service founded in 2021 by Brian McMahon and Julia O'Mara, offers its predominantly Gen Z and millennial customers access to luxury clothing and accessories at a fraction of the purchasing cost. Last month, a Pickle user even earned $30,000 on the app, says McMahon, who is the cofounder and CEO.

title: South Korea orders residents to evacuate after reported white phosphorus leak at US base
description: South Korean authorities ordered civilians to evacuate on Tuesday after a suspected white phosphorus leak at a U.S. military base near the capital, Seoul.  Officials in the city of Pyeongtaek urged ne...
fullText:
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korean authorities ordered civilians to evacuate on Tuesday after a suspected white phosphorus leak at a U.S. military base near the capital, Seoul.

Officials in the city of Pyeongtaek urged nearby residents to move to a safe location and avoid skin exposure after the leak at the Osan Air Base was detected at around 5 p.m. The alert was lifted several hours later following the completion of decontamination work, according to text messages sent out by the city.

The U.S. 51st Fighter Wing said it established a 300-meter cordon around the base "out of an abundance of caution" after experts conducting a routine inspection identified white phosphorus crystallization that left residue inside a munitions crate.

An explosive ordnance disposal unit was deployed and response plans were immediately activated to ensure the munitions remained fully contained, it said in a statement.

The cordon was lifted after emergency response personnel mitigated the situation, allowing the base to return to normal operations, it said. There were "no injuries resulting from this situation and no risk to personnel on or off installation."

"The safety of our service members, their families, and our Pyeongtaek neighbors remains our absolute highest priority," said base commander Col. Ryan Ley.

White phosphorus is a controversial chemical substance used in incendiary munitions and smoke shells. When ignited, it burns at extremely high temperatures and can set buildings ablaze and burn human flesh to the bone.

title: Their land was taken centuries ago. Now the Pamunkey tribe is getting it back.
description: The 13 acres overlooking the river that bears their name have long been a part of the Pamunkey Indian Tribe’s ancestral homeland. The land in King William County, Virginia, was taken from them centuri...
fullText:
The 13 acres overlooking the river that bears their name have long been a part of the Pamunkey Indian Tribe's ancestral homeland.

The land in King William County, Virginia, was taken from them centuries ago, but through a recent $1.9 million deal, the tribe regained ownership and plans to expand its cultural and economic presence in the region.

The return of the land marks a milestone for the Pamunkey tribe, which gained federal recognition in 2015 and has roughly 530 enrolled members. The purchase also reflects a broader movement by Native nations across the country to reclaim territorial lands lost through broken treaties, forced dispossession and private acquisition.

Known as Windsor Shades estate, the property - about two hours south of Washington - has a long history. It was for centuries one of several villages where Pamunkey chiefs lived, and it was called Kupkipcock in the Powhatan Algonquin language. English explorer John Smith documented it in an early 1600s map of Native American villages. The property later became a Revolutionary War landmark. It remained in private ownership for decades.

"This is land that was taken from us in the 17th century, and getting it back now is righting a historical wrong," said Ashley Atkins Spivey, a citizen of the Pamunkey tribe and an anthropologist. "This land was ours for thousands and thousands of years, and the non-Indigenous occupation of it is a blip in time, compared to the relationship and connection our people have to it."

Officials with the Pamunkey tribe said they're considering plans to use the land to provide cultural, educational and economic opportunities, possibly using it as an event space or partnering with an operator to host wine tastings.

When the deal closed in May, Pamunkey Chief Kevin Brown said that the purchase was "more than a real estate transaction; it is an act of historical recognition and cultural preservation."

Two other Virginia tribes have also recently regained pieces of their homelands. The Rappahannock tribe closed a deal for 700 acres, part of a decade-long effort to reclaim more than 2,000 acres in an area known as Fones Cliffs in Richmond County. Earlier this month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an agreement placing 28 acres of land in King William County that were once part of the Mattaponi Indian Tribe's original land into a state trust for the tribe.

At Windsor Shades, archaeological evidence shows that the Pamunkeys occupied the site long before English settlers arrived. Pamunkey tribal chiefs, including Opechancanough - the younger brother of Powhatan, one of the most famous and powerful Native chiefs on the East Coast - lived there with their families. Nearby, other Pamunkey communities helped produce food and paid tribute to the chiefs and their families.

Smith referred to the village as "a king house" in his writings and on his map, historians said.

"It's profoundly meaningful that this property is returning to the Pamunkey tribe," said Jennie Dotts, the Long & Foster real estate agent who represented the tribe. "It was their land originally, and now it is theirs once again. That's a satisfying sense of history coming full circle."

Around 1640, the property Windsor Shades became part of a roughly 5,000-acre land grant awarded to English settler William Claiborne by the Virginia colony after his forces defeated the Pamunkeys in battle, according to historians and the real estate company involved in the sale.

Built in the mid-1700s, the house on the property is one of Virginia's best-preserved examples of an 18th-century Tidewater structure. The property became well-known in the 1750s after a ferry was established there and a tavern opened in the English basement of the house, with an outside stairway entrance. Historians believe that George Washington stopped regularly at the tavern while traveling between Mount Vernon and Williamsburg, based on a dozen entries in his diaries.

In 1781, the Marquis de Lafayette and his troops crossed the Pamunkey River at Ruffin's Ferry on the property before heading to the Battle of Yorktown.

Windsor Shades, about 15 minutes from the tribe's reservation, later became a tobacco plantation and was eventually placed under a historic easement. The five-bedroom brick house features several chimneys. The spot where the tavern was is now a dining room and contains what Dotts said is one of Virginia's largest interior fireplaces, with an eight-foot opening. Dotts said she specializes in historic properties and "rarely comes across one so historically intact and meticulously preserved."

Windsor Shades is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is named as a Virginia historic landmark.

The sale came about after one of Atkins Spivey's research associates, who serves on a local historical board and is married to a Pamunkey tribal member, learned that Carl and Lynn Fischer, who had owned Windsor Shades since the late 1990s, planned to put it on the market. Brown, the tribal chief, became involved in the spring.

Tribal leaders said it is unfortunate that so much time passed before they were able to reacquire Windsor Shades, but they are relieved to have it back in Native hands.

"It took so long because we were dealing with massive amounts of European colonial expansion, and we didn't have the capacity to fight that army of invaders," Atkins Spivey said. "While we've been able to survive, we didn't have the funds or resources to buy a piece of land back until recently. Now we have the economic capacity to do that."

title: Former college soccer player found dead off San Diego beach in one of nation's wealthiest beach communities
description: Bryn Waite, a former Central Washington University soccer player from Anchorage, was found dead in waters off La Jolla Shores Beach in San Diego.
fullText:
A former college soccer player has been identified as the 26-year-old woman found dead in the waters off San Diego's La Jolla Shores Beach as investigators work to determine what happened.

Emergency personnel responded around 9:30 a.m. Wednesday after reports of an unresponsive person floating in shallow water, the San Diego County Medical Examiner's Office said. Bryn Waite was pronounced dead at the scene.

The body was found near the Ellen Browning Scripps Memorial Pier, FOX 5 San Diego reported.

Sled Joins Probe As Body Matching Missing South Carolina Personal Trainer's Description Found

Officers and lifeguards with San Diego Fire-Rescue responded after a bystander spotted the woman in the water, the station added. Fire officials said the San Diego Police Department would lead the investigation.

The Medical Examiner identified the woman as Waite and said her cause and manner of death remain pending investigation by the San Diego Police Department. The office listed her place of injury as "Ocean – Undetermined" and said the date and time of injury are unknown.

Originally from Anchorage, Alaska, Waite played defender at Central Washington University during the 2018 and 2019 seasons. She appeared in 15 games, making eight starts, and tallied two assists over 723 career minutes. Waite earned Great Northwest Athletic Conference All-Academic Team honors in 2019.

Former College Soccer Player Killed In Boat Crash After Group Allegedly Took Vessel Without Authorization

Friends told The California Post that Waite had been living in San Diego and had recently gotten engaged.

"I only met Bryn a couple of times, but each time she was incredibly sweet, genuinely kind and had such a beautiful spirit," one friend told the outlet.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

"She had a warmth about her that made people feel comfortable and cared for," the friend said. "It's clear that the light she carried touched so many lives. She will be deeply missed."

Another friend, who said she knew Waite through church and had seen her recently, described her as "kind and sweet."

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

"She listened and loved," the friend told the Post. "She is leaving behind friends and family that will miss her dearly."

Cause Of Death Revealed For Big Sur Hiker Whose Body Was Found Naked On Remote California Trail

The friend added that Waite "loved animals and the beach."

Waite's public Instagram account included photos from Joshua Tree National Park and other travels. Her final post, shared three days before she was found, featured a nighttime photo with the caption, "It only gets better."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Investigators have not said how Waite ended up in the water or whether foul play is suspected. The circumstances surrounding her death remain under investigation.

The Medical Examiner's Office has not released an estimated time of death, and authorities have not said whether Waite had been reported missing before her body was discovered.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the San Diego Police Department, San Diego Fire-Rescue, the San Diego County Medical Examiner's Office and Central Washington University and will update this story as more information becomes available.
